ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Will stands at a point $P$ on the edge of a circular room with perfectly reflective walls. He shines two laser pointers into the room, forming angles of $n^o$ and $(n + 1)^o$ with the tangent at $P$, where $n$ is a positive integer less than $90$. The lasers reflect off of the walls, illuminating the points they hit on the walls, until they reach $P$ again. ($P$ is also illuminated at the end.) What is the minimum possible number of illuminated points on the walls of the room?\n<image1>

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a circular room with a tangent line at point P and laser paths reflecting inside the circle; it illustrates that each laser travels along chords and reflects off the circular wall. Reasoning: Model the boundary hits as positions on a cyclic group. If a laser leaves P making angle a degrees with the tangent, then the chord to the next wall point subtends a central angle of 2a degrees. Therefore each successive reflection advances by 2a degrees around the circle. Since a is an integer degree, dividing all central angles by 2 lets us work in Z_180, where the hit set is the subgroup generated by a. Thus the number of distinct wall points hit by the laser with angle a, including P, is T(a) = 180 / gcd(180, a). For the two lasers, the total illuminated points are |S_n union S_{n+1}| = T(n) + T(n+1) - |S_n intersection S_{n+1}|. Because these hit sets are subgroups of the cyclic group Z_180, their intersection has size gcd(T(n), T(n+1)). Let d = gcd(180, n) and e = gcd(180, n+1). Since n and n+1 are consecutive, d and e are coprime divisors of 180. Then T(n) = 180/d, T(n+1) = 180/e. We need minimize 180/d + 180/e - gcd(180/d, 180/e). Since d and e are coprime divisors of 180 = 2^2 * 3^2 * 5, the best split is d = 20 and e = 9. This is feasible because n = 80 gives gcd(180, 80) = 20 and gcd(180, 81) = 9. For n = 80: T(80) = 180/20 = 9, T(81) = 180/9 = 20, and the intersection size is gcd(9, 20) = 1. So the union contains 9 + 20 - 1 = 28 illuminated points. Therefore the minimum possible number of illuminated wall points is 28.

method.method_draft: Use a cyclic-group model of the billiard path. From the geometry, a ray making angle a degrees with the tangent advances by central angle 2a degrees between successive wall hits, so its illuminated wall points correspond to the subgroup generated by 2a in angles modulo 360, equivalently by a in Z_180. Thus the number of distinct points for angle a, including P, is T(a)=180/gcd(180,a). For the two lasers, the total number is |S_n union S_{n+1}|=T(n)+T(n+1)-|S_n intersection S_{n+1}|. Since these are subgroups of a cyclic group, the intersection size is gcd(T(n),T(n+1)). Now set d=gcd(180,n) and e=gcd(180,n+1). Because n and n+1 are consecutive, d and e are coprime divisors of 180. Minimize 180/d+180/e-gcd(180/d,180/e) over feasible coprime divisor pairs, using 180=2^2*3^2*5. The best feasible split is d=20, e=9, realized by n=80, giving T(80)=9 and T(81)=20 with intersection size 1, so the union has 9+20-1=28 points.

method.method_draft: Use a candidate-elimination table based on possible short periods. First derive the period rule geometrically: a laser at tangent angle a degrees hits vertices of a regular star polygon with period T(a)=180/gcd(180,a). Exhibit n=80: the two periods are T(80)=9 and T(81)=20; their common illuminated points number gcd(9,20)=1, so they illuminate 9+20-1=28 points. To prove this is minimal, suppose a total below 28 were possible. Then each individual laser would have to have fewer than 28 illuminated points, so gcd(180,a)>180/28, i.e. gcd(180,a) is at least 9. Make a short table of angles a from 1 to 90 with T(a)<28: 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 27, 30, 36, 40, 45, 48, 50, 54, 60, 63, 70, 72, 75, 80, 81, 84, 90. The only consecutive pairs in this list are (9,10) and (80,81). For (9,10), the periods are 20 and 18 and the union size is 20+18-gcd(20,18)=36. For (80,81), the union size is 28. Hence no value below 28 can occur, and 28 is achieved.
method.CoT_raw:
The image illustrates the setup: a circular room, a point P on the wall, a tangent at P, and laser paths reflecting along chords. No numerical information is needed from the image.

Geometric period rule: If a laser leaves P making angle a° with the tangent, then by the tangent-chord theorem the chord to the next wall point subtends central angle 2a°. After each reflection, the same angle with the tangent is preserved, so the hit points advance around the circle by 2a° each time. Thus the laser returns to P when k·2a is a multiple of 360, so the period is T(a)=360/gcd(360,2a)=180/gcd(180,a). This period is the number of distinct illuminated wall points for that laser, including P.

For two lasers with periods T1 and T2 starting at the same point P, each set of hit points is a regular polygon vertex set based at P. Their common illuminated points number gcd(T1,T2), so the total union size is T1+T2−gcd(T1,T2).

Exhibit n=80. Then the angles are 80° and 81°. T(80)=180/gcd(180,80)=180/20=9, and T(81)=180/gcd(180,81)=180/9=20. Their overlap has gcd(9,20)=1 point, so the total illuminated points are 9+20−1=28.

Now prove no smaller total is possible. If the total were below 28, then each individual laser would have fewer than 28 illuminated points, so T(a)<28 for each angle a. Since T(a)=180/gcd(180,a), this requires gcd(180,a)>180/28, so gcd(180,a) is at least 9. Checking angles a from 1 to 90 with T(a)<28 gives: 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 27, 30, 36, 40, 45, 48, 50, 54, 60, 63, 70, 72, 75, 80, 81, 84, 90. The only consecutive pairs in this list are (9,10) and (80,81).

For (9,10), the periods are T(9)=20 and T(10)=18, so the union size is 20+18−gcd(20,18)=20+18−2=36. For (80,81), the union size is 28 as shown. Therefore no value below 28 can occur, and 28 is achieved.

He shines two laser pointers into the room, forming angles of $n^\circ$ and $(n+1)^\circ$ with the tangent at $P$, where $n$ is a positive integer less than $90$. The lasers reflect off the walls, illuminating the points they hit on the walls, until they reach $P$ again. ($P$ is also illuminated at the end.) What is the minimum possible number of illuminated points on the walls of the room?
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The diagram shows a circular room with a tangent line at point P and laser paths reflecting inside the circle; it illustrates that each laser travels along chords and reflects off the circular wall.

Reasoning: Model the boundary hits as positions on a cyclic group. If a laser leaves P making angle a degrees with the tangent, then the chord to the next wall point subtends a central angle of 2a degrees. Therefore each successive reflection advances by 2a degrees around the circle. Since a is an integer degree, dividing all central angles by 2 lets us work in Z_180, where the hit set is the subgroup generated by a.

Thus the number of distinct wall points hit by the laser with angle a, including P, is
T(a) = 180 / gcd(180, a).

For the two lasers, the total illuminated points are
|S_n union S_{n+1}| = T(n) + T(n+1) - |S_n intersection S_{n+1}|.
Because these hit sets are subgroups of the cyclic group Z_180, their intersection has size gcd(T(n), T(n+1)).

Let d = gcd(180, n) and e = gcd(180, n+1). Since n and n+1 are consecutive, d and e are coprime divisors of 180. Then
T(n) = 180/d, T(n+1) = 180/e.
We need minimize
180/d + 180/e - gcd(180/d, 180/e).
Since d and e are coprime divisors of 180 = 2^2 * 3^2 * 5, the best split is d = 20 and e = 9. This is feasible because n = 80 gives gcd(180, 80) = 20 and gcd(180, 81) = 9.

For n = 80:
T(80) = 180/20 = 9,
T(81) = 180/9 = 20,
and the intersection size is gcd(9, 20) = 1.
So the union contains
9 + 20 - 1 = 28
illuminated points.

Therefore the minimum possible number of illuminated wall points is 28.
